visual_features.distinctive_marks: Scaly texture with visible grooves and patterns on the head and body

description: The Komodo dragon (also known as the Komodo monitor) is a large reptile of the monitor lizard family Varanidae, endemic to the Indonesian islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami, and Gili Motang. It is the largest living lizard species and an apex predator with unique group hunting behavior. Its diet consists mainly of Javan rusa deer and feral pigs, though it also eats carrion and can take down water buffalo. It is one of the few venomous lizards, with venom glands in its lower jaw. Adults have no natural predators. Juveniles are arboreal to avoid cannibalism. They take 8-11 years to mature and live up to 30-62 years. Mating occurs May-August, eggs laid in September with hatching in April. First documented by Western scientists in 1910.
population_estimate: Approximately 3,500 total individuals including adults and juveniles (2021 estimate), with ~1,400 mature individuals. About 400 mature females. Two-thirds occur on Komodo and Rinca Islands (Komodo National Park: ~2,450; Rinca: ~1,100-1,500). Flores has scattered populations (~100 in Wae Waul Reserve, ~2,000 in non-protected areas). Gili Motang and Nusa Kode have fewer than 100 each. Eight subpopulations each with fewer than 500 individuals. Status changed from Vulnerable to Endangered in 2021. CITES Appendix I. Protected under Indonesian law since the 1930s.
habitat: Endemic to the Indonesian islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Dasami, and Gili Motang. Komodo National Park (UNESCO World Heritage site) protects the largest population. Adults inhabit tropical savannah forests and open grasslands with scattered trees. Juveniles live in trees. Found from beach areas to mountain slopes. The species experienced 44% range contraction on Flores over 5 years due to habitat destruction.
threats: Habitat destruction from logging and agricultural expansion
Illegal trafficking for exotic pet trade (up to 98% of transactions via social media)
Climate change and rising sea levels threatening island habitats
Forest fires started by poachers to flush out prey
Poaching of prey species (deer, wild boar)
44% range area contraction on Flores Island over 5 years
Small isolated subpopulations vulnerable to inbreeding and genetic drift
Volcanic ash deposition can destroy vegetation and alter habitat
ecosystem_role: Apex predator that dominates the ecosystems it inhabits. It controls populations of large mammals (deer, wild boar, water buffalo). Its scavenging of carrion helps with nutrient cycling. Group hunting behavior is exceptional among reptiles. As one of the largest animals in its habitat, it has no natural predators as an adult.
human_connection: An iconic species of Indonesia and major ecotourism attraction at Komodo National Park. Protected by Indonesian law since the 1930s. Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1991. Occasionally attacks humans. Scientific study began in 1910; the species inspired the 1933 film 'King Kong'. Conservation efforts include community-based patrols, environmental education, and ecotourism revenue sharing with local communities. Economic value from tourism motivates local protection efforts.
what_students_can_do: Learn about Komodo dragon conservation and the UNESCO World Heritage Komodo National Park
Support responsible ecotourism that benefits local communities
Never purchase exotic pets from illegal wildlife trade - reptiles are not pets
Spread awareness about how climate change threatens island-endemic species
Support organizations working on Komodo dragon habitat protection
fun_fact: The Komodo dragon is the heaviest lizard on Earth - the largest captive specimen weighed 166 kg (366 lb).
It is one of the few venomous lizards, with venom glands in its lower jaw that cause prey to go into shock and lower blood pressure.
Young Komodo dragons roll in feces to deter cannibalistic adults from eating them.
The species inspired the 1933 movie 'King Kong' - W. Douglas Burden's expedition brought the first live specimens back to the US.
It is locally known as 'ora' or 'buaya darat' (land crocodile) by the people of Komodo Island.
